claims.text: Adding a controlled fraction of targeted oxide-forming elements to a lightweight high-entropy alloy produces a coherent nanoscale oxide dispersion.
A coherent nanoscale oxide dispersion impedes dislocation motion.
The oxide-forming additions generate a stable passivating surface.
The proposed oxide dispersion and passivating surface enhance mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
An optimized heat treatment precipitates a fine, coherent oxide dispersion after homogeneous addition of oxide-forming elements.
During heat treatment, the added oxide-forming elements react to form finely dispersed oxide particles.
The dispersed oxide particles pin dislocations and thereby increase strength.
Oxides coalescing at the alloy surface form a stable passivating layer.
The passivating layer protects the alloy against corrosion and high-temperature oxidation.
Relative to the baseline alloy, the modified alloy will exhibit increased yield strength.
Relative to the baseline alloy, the modified alloy will exhibit reduced oxidation mass gain.
Relative to the baseline alloy, the modified alloy will exhibit lower corrosion rates.
The mechanism will cease to hold if the oxide dispersion becomes too coarse or loses coherence.
Excessive oxide-forming-element concentration or inadequately optimized heat treatment can cause oxide coarsening, loss of coherence, embrittlement, or harmful secondary phases.
Oxidizing and corrosive environments above 600 degrees Celsius are representative of the targeted aerospace and rail applications.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described as untreated, but the experiment states that both modified and baseline samples receive the same processing and heat treatment.

Coarse or non-coherent oxides are defined as conditions under which the mechanism should cease to hold, yet observing such particles is also treated as falsifying the hypothesis. A result obtained outside the stated validity regime would not by itself falsify the mechanism.
